newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Western envoy seeks to avert fresh Albania crisis.
newsitem.headline: Western envoy seeks to avert fresh Albania crisis.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky is due to arrive on an emergency mission to the Balkan state of Albania on Thursday, seeking to stop the country sliding into crisis by getting early elections back on course.

Vranitzky's fifth visit to Albania takes place amid hopes a new crisis over the elections can be averted after President Sali Berisha on Wednesday postponed a decree to call the vote, which most political parties had threatened to boycott.
The elections are seen as vital to make sure Albania does not plunge back into the unrest and violence of February and March after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.

Vranitzky, acting on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), is to meet Berisha, Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and other key leaders in a hastily-arranged one-day visit.
Western diplomats said there was cautious optimism that the planned elections could be put back on course.
"There are signs of a compromise," one diplomat said.
Vrantizky brokered a six-point political contract last week, under which the nine main parties agreed to pass a new electoral law and then call a vote for the end of June.
But a fresh crisis blew up as most of the parties of a nine-party interim Government of National Reconciliation refused to stand in the elections.
They said Berisha's Democrat Party had pushed a law through parliament which the parties said was tilted in their favour.
They were also furious the law was presented by the Democrats rather than the government.
The other parties were also unhappy over the division of seats between proportional representation and majority voting.

The new crisis seemed certain after Berisha on Wednesday promised to supporters that he would dissolve parliament and call the elections despite the threatened boycott. But his office later said he had postponed the decree.
The parties, led by the Socialists, want more seats on a proportional basis while the Democratic Party favours more majority voting.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.
The Democratic Party insisted its law was in line with last week's Vranitzky deal and agreements with other parties.

Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees, formed mostly in the south of the country at the time of the rioting to bring back order as the state administration collapsed.

The contract said they should disband 46 days before the election, but they have said they will break up only if the elections are guaranteed to be free and fair. A meeting of the committees is due on Friday.
